**July 4, 2026

** This year, we celebrate the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, whose main author was Thomas Jefferson.

But some Americans do not believe America is great and see little reason to celebrate. They believe our country was built on racism, slavery and sexism. But what they do not realize is that they are free to say this without the fear of arrest, imprisonment or even worse, ironically proving that America is great.
> We Americans love to celebrate our diversity. We have Columbus Day, St. Patrick's Day and Martin Luther King Day. Various ethnic groups have parades to honor their culture; and this is fine. But we often forget about the one group to whom we owe our freedom and prosperity - the Anglo-Saxons.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/f2f01fbf-ea79-4cfe-bbac-ca390638aedf?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
King Charles III
> Tenth century England was a primitive place. It was barely an Iron Age culture, with marauding tribes engaged in internecine struggles among themselves and against the invading Vikings. Illiteracy was the norm. Meanwhile, Japan had established an advanced culture of writing and literature. Thirteenth century China built ships ten times the size of those Columbus used to cross the Atlantic. The Arab world invented algebra, advanced architecture and a body of literature that delights children to this day. Meanwhile, the English survived by subsistence farming, lived in huts and walked around in clothing that was nothing more than a burlap sack. Yet the people from this small island established global hegemony. Why? Because while other cultures lived under Rule of Men, the English developed Rule of Law.
> Ever since King John was forced to sign the Magna Carta at Runnymede in 1215, the English people chipped away at privilege and power, enabling all citizens to be equal in the eyes of the Law. The Magna Carta allowed heirs to inherit property without confiscation by the State. It ended the practice of forcing wealthy widows to marry politically connected nobility and merchants. Parliament was eventually established. The much maligned Richard III promulgated the concept of a free press and bail for the accused. [The Petition of Right in 1628](https://substack.com/redirect/702bac97-1031-4c7d-9e4f-eb55ac9cefdd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) prohibited excessive taxation and the quartering of soldiers in one's house. It created the concept of habeas corpus - meaning you could not be arrested without being accused of a crime. The English fought for the right to bear arms, worship freely and not have to pay damages for a crime one did not commit. These became known as the Rights of Englishmen and when King George III refused to extend these rights to the American colonies, our forefathers rebelled.
> It has become fashionable among our cultural elite to disparage our forefathers as racists, homophobes, misogynists and elitists. But they were great men. The entire planet dreams of living in England or one of its children - whether it be the United States, Canada, Australia or New Zealand. Iran does not have an illegal immigration problem.
> So this Fourth of July, permit me to raise a glass of cognac to the man who sailed to Sicily and convinced my grandfather and my great uncles to immigrate to the United States and work in the coal mines of Pennsylvania. My grandfather despised this man, disparaging him with the term "Johnny Bull." He felt he had been deceived as this life-threatening, back breaking work paid poorly. But when my grandfather made money, he got to keep it. And when he built a house for my grandmother, my father and his five siblings; no Mafia thug could take it away from him. And his children became college professors. And his grandchildren became doctors and lawyers. And his great grandchildren went to fine universities and live a life style and have opportunities my grandfather could never have conceived.
> So I hope the descendants of this man are as fat and happy as we are; and I hope that at some time in my career, one of his descendants came into my office, shook my hand and thanked me when I handled his eye problem competently.
>

# [](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/126?t=1&akid=7537%2E582294%2EA1SHc4)
I joined Jen Psaki tonight to talk about why New Hampshire is shaping up to be one of the most important Senate races in the country.
[](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260703_2.um_0Tv&refcode=em20260703-2&t=2&akid=7537%2E582294%2EA1SHc4)
**The fight for the Senate majority could come down to what happens right here in the Granite State.**
Republicans know this race is one of their best opportunities to flip a seat. That's why they're already pouring millions into New Hampshire and planning to spend millions more.
We can win this race – but only if we keep building the kind of grassroots campaign that has powered us from the very beginning.
After my conversation with Jen on the stakes of this race, I need to ask: **[Can you chip in $25, or whatever you can, to help us keep this momentum going and show that New Hampshire is ready for this fight?](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260703_2.um_0Tv&refcode=em20260703-2&t=3&akid=7537%2E582294%2EA1SHc4)**

I've spent my career fighting to lower costs for working families, protect our fundamental freedoms, and make government work for the people it's supposed to serve – not the wealthy and well-connected.
That's what's at stake in this election.
The national attention on our race is only going to grow from here, and the attacks and outside spending will grow right alongside it. We need to be prepared for everything that's coming.
**[If you're with me, please make a contribution of $25 or whatever you can to my campaign today.](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260703_2.um_0Tv&refcode=em20260703-2&t=23&akid=7537%2E582294%2EA1SHc4)**

subject: Happy 250th Birthday, America! 🇺🇸
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Collins for Senator
body:
May we continue to stand strong and united.

|

Peter, Today, we celebrate an extraordinary milestone in our nation's history: the 250th anniversary of the founding of the United States of America.Two and a half centuries ago, our Founders embarked on a bold experiment in self-government founded on the enduring principles of liberty, equality, and opportunity. Through times of triumph and challenge alike, generations of Americans have worked to preserve those ideals and strengthen our democracy.From the rocky coast of Maine to communities across our great nation, Americans have always shown remarkable resilience, generosity, and determination. Our differences have never diminished our shared commitment to freedom, opportunity, and the promise that hard work and perseverance can build a better future.It is the honor of my lifetime to represent the people of Maine in the United States Senate. Every day, I am inspired by the independence, kindness, and strength of Mainers, and I remain committed to working on their behalf and helping to ensure that our state and our nation continue to thrive.As we gather with family, friends, and neighbors this Independence Day, let us celebrate all that unites us, reflect on the sacrifices made by those who came before us, and look ahead with confidence and hope.Happy 250th Birthday, America. May God continue to bless our great nation.Warmly,Susan CollinsU.S. Senator for Maine

Friends, Today, like every day, is a great day to be an American. Our nation’s semiquincentennial is a special opportunity to reflect on the courage of our Founding Fathers, the sacrifices of our service members and President Ronald Reagan’s wise words and stark warning that “freedom is never more than one generation away from extinction.”
---
It is up to each of us to ensure that our country continues to prosper so, 250 years from now, our descendants can also celebrate freedom.
---
As the daughter of immigrants, one of whom fled communism, I know how special this country is and why America remains the greatest nation on Earth. That is why I am thankful to my constituents for giving me the opportunity to represent Staten Island and Southern Brooklyn in Congress and appreciate all of your unwavering support throughout my years in public service. I look forward to celebrating this historic milestone with our community, honoring the values that unite us, and recommitting ourselves to preserving the freedoms and liberties that generations of Americans have fought to protect. I wish you and your family a Happy Independence Day, and God Bless the United States of America. Your fellow patriot, Nicole

name: Marsha Blackburn
subject: Happy 4th of July, Peter! 🇺🇲
body:
Today, we celebrate 250 years of freedom!

| | | | | | Peter,
Today, we celebrate 250 years of freedom! 250 years!
Let's take a moment to appreciate the freedom and opportunities that make America the greatest country on earth!
We're reminded of the brave men and women who fought for our independence 250 years ago, and the sacrifices they made to build our nation.
As we celebrate this historic milestone, I hope you can relax, enjoy some good food and company, and celebrate what it means to be an American!
From my family to yours, have a happy, safe, and historic 4th of July! 🇺🇸
May God bless you and the United States of America,
Marsha Blackburn

name: Troy Downing
subject: Happy Fourth of July!
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Troy Downing for Congress
body:
Today, we celebrate 250 years of American independence.

| [](https://trk.emails.troydowning._ZI6Q02s9cmQ)
---
Peter,As we gather with family, friends, and neighbors to celebrate the Fourth of July, I want to wish you and your loved ones a safe, joyful, and happy Independence Day.Today, we celebrate 250 years of American independence and the enduring spirit of liberty that defines our great nation. It is a time to reflect on the incredible blessings of freedom we enjoy and to honor the brave men and women in uniform – past and present – who have sacrificed so much to protect those freedoms.Whether you are enjoying a backyard barbecue, watching fireworks, or spending time outdoors, I hope your holiday is filled with American pride, reflection, and community.Thank you for your continued support, and may God bless the United States of America.In Liberty,Troy Downing (MT-02)

name: Jen Kiggans
subject: Happy Birthday, America! 🇺🇸
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Kiggans for Congress
body:
It’s Independence Day!

| | | | | | 🇺🇸 Happy Independence Day!!! 🇺🇸Today marks a historic milestone - 250 years since the signing of the Declaration of Independence in 1776! America is the land of freedom, opportunity, and enduring patriotism. This has always been my favorite holiday for a few personal reasons - my husband and I were engaged on July 4th at the base of the Washington Monument, and I absolutely love seeing our communities blanketed in red, white, and blue.
---
---
But this year feels even more incredible as we celebrate a quarter-millennium of American liberty!As a Navy veteran, this milestone hits close to home for me. I think about the generations of ordinary citizens who possessed the extraordinary courage to fight for our founding ideals, and the generations of heroes who have stepped up to defend them ever since. We are profoundly blessed to inherit the freedom they secured.America remains the greatest nation in the world, and it is the honor of a lifetime to celebrate her landmark 250th birthday alongside all of you.Hopefully, you can spend some time with your family and friends today to honor our great nation and the freedoms we enjoy. As we celebrate this historic milestone, let us also take extra time to appreciate the brave men and women who have served and continue to serve our country to keep us free.
May God continue to Bless America!Happy 250th Birthday to the USA!!! 🎉🇺🇸
---
---
\- Jen Kiggans

# Saturday, July 4, 2026
---|---
**Happy Fourth of July!** On this day in 1776, the Continental Congress formally adopted the Declaration of Independence, announcing the American colonies' separation from Great Britain and [giving birth to a new nation](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0DGOqzAQgOHTmC5oPHYAFy5eQ5fXbokcPISJHIzs2SBuv8peYetf-or_6zbdAifeHv_Di7wsedroqIlEqEy8Rdppi7TNFMO5UpB7ClXKhIDdBfoL2CkGTudkm-gXIiTTkNf9YPTVDQaa1QORQ3SddQtZMLOJYKzuEOcruHi_N-w_GvRgNWjAvtV26LULA0WDiw5OWaDIkkv7zLzJSks685tKO-dXk_wqsldl_ikcFY7HcbQrV8nl_HSFYyjCc6KqcHx-p_NiZW2Kj_vBKXHtemXh8Qqcfjn504O3x58AAAD__w6Gb7g).

As our nation commemorates its 250th birthday this weekend, we'll be sending out shortened editions through Monday so _The Flyover _staff can celebrate the holiday with friends and family. Our regular edition will return on Tuesday. Have a safe and happy Fourth of July weekend! Are you the one setting off fireworks, or the one lying awake wishing they'd stop? Somewhere on your street tonight, someone's going till midnight while the dog shakes under the bed and half the block wonders if they're the only ones who've had enough. Fireworks are the sound of the Fourth, the whole country looking up at once. But they're also sparking wildfire fears, veterans bracing at every crack, and thousands of ER visits a year. So are they worth it? Tune in to today's _Flyover Podcast_ as Amy shares both sides of the story. Which side are you on? ## Rare 'Declaration' Copy Found in London
A volunteer at Britain's National Archives has discovered a [rare 1776 printing](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkDGvpSAUhH8NdhhAvUhBsY3d3XZLc4TD9exywSBX47_f-KrXv24yk0zmmz_P-QkUKb1-wxttDXlOeO4Ra8UyU_K4YfKYHHq4VoS6RNhrmZVQDy40F_3sgeI19423AVFh16CVeuzkYMZONKs18qEXufSD6YwCHKReQPtghPJucOPYkL3bhBa9FFIo3cp-1NLAiL5TQYJhvUBPNZf2b6ZUVwzxygeW1uV3E-1a67az7hdTE1PTeZ6tW_ab4s6Zmm7J1HRAon2l9IoXL1CQu7xdPAdeV-QeXYQClXK6re_gPORP8pwS__B_fLn4keMnVcTC1NQU67eTYqT9oVkvXm-g-LWr_ujMw6r_AQAA__-USIsf) of the Declaration of Independence, one of only 11 surviving "Exeter Declarations" and the only copy known outside the United States. The document was [seized on Christmas Eve 1776](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLGOszAQhJ8GOiN7bQIULv6GLn97Jdp418F3jo2ME5S3P3HV9dfOSKP5vo_rcsUQQ7r_xwfb6vOS-Ngj18plCYl440ScHBO-V8Z6i7jXsoCEi5CDkGYhDPG9mJasZwbWLVs1jFr106hlu1pwdGOSGidPiJLYe_Ra6qm_GO96boM91-QgjZJKwtApMw5qwpFJg1c4NUYyhZpL95lDqiv7-M4vLp3LjzbatdZtb_S_BuYG5uM4unRzJ8XZn0kukRqY-Vnyxg3MBQsLYhexYA05id-cwudnIhGSeH6J4hLqHsYe2mJpO0KMYb8MjZH3B4b4c6D-ydrLwncAAAD__3bWgxM) when the Royal Navy captured the American privateer _Dalton_ off Portugal after a seven-hour chase. Logged simply as "another paper," it sat unnoticed for 250 years. "Exeter Declarations" are a specific batch of early printed copies of the Declaration of Independence, produced by printer Robert Luist Fowle in Exeter, New Hampshire, between July 16 and 19, 1776, roughly two weeks after the original was adopted in Philadelphia on July 4. Volunteer Michael Scurr found it while cataloguing Navy correspondence. It will go on display in the Archives' [Revolution 250 exhibition](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkDHznCAQRz8NdjiA-ucoKNLYXdqUzh4sSrIHDqLGb5_xqqRO-2bnzf7ej-f0hEgxzd_hjbaGPCU8N8JasUwxeVwxeUwOPVwLQn0RbLVMSqgvLjQX_eQh0jX1jbcBUWHXoJX60cnBPDrRLHboX3LQ2gwQOjNoOSjAlxTGKRmMML6J9rYJLXoppFC6lf1DSwMP9J0KEgzrBfpYc2l_5pjqgoGufGBpXX43ZJda141135gamRrP82wT1JgTEBS3xAO3ds5Hu_9iasTfK-WCvC7IXSZCd18yNf4L-IvyzNQYSn7zvBd-ZNpTRSzbTWPyMc0ceMKTu7xePIePct-4R0dQPg_c9O-ETI1NsX49I1HcvjTrxfyGSJ8d9b_iH1b9CQAA__9qGJzK), running through November.

250 Years of the Greatest Experiment on Earth
Two hundred and fifty years ago, a group of ordinary men did something extraordinary. They looked at the most powerful empire in the world and said no. Not because they were sure they would win. Not because it was safe or easy. Because they believed, with everything they had, that men were created to be free. That idea changed the world. It still does.
America is not perfect. She never has been. But she is the greatest experiment in self-governance this world has ever seen, and every generation has been asked to prove that the experiment still works. Some generations fought wars to do it. Some fought in courtrooms and town halls and precinct meetings. Some knocked doors and made phone calls and showed up when it would have been easier to stay home. That is what it means to be an American. Not just to inherit this republic, but to earn it. Every single day.
Republicans have understood that from the very beginning. It was a Republican president, Abraham Lincoln, who held this nation together when it was tearing itself apart, who issued the Emancipation Proclamation and fought to pass the 13th Amendment abolishing slavery. It was Theodore Roosevelt who took on the monopolies and the machine politicians who had rigged the system against the working man. It was Ronald Reagan who looked a crumbling Soviet empire in the eye and called it what it was, who cut taxes, championed the free market, and reminded a generation of Americans that government is not the solution to our problems. Republicans have never been perfect. But when the republic has needed someone to stand in the gap, we have shown up.
And we are needed again right now.
Ronald Reagan said it best: freedom is never more than one generation away from extinction. It must be fought for, protected, and handed on. He was right then. He is right now. There are forces at work in our own backyard and across this country that do not believe in what this flag stands for. They do not believe in your right to own property, run your business, raise your children by your own values, or live your life without a bureaucrat telling you how.
We believe in all of those things. That is why we fight.
So this Fourth of July, fly your flag. Mean it. Teach your kids what it costs. Two hundred and fifty years. Not because it was guaranteed. Because Americans kept choosing it.
Let's keep choosing it.
Together, We Win!
In Liberty and in Truth, Mary Jane Truemper Chairman, Nebraska Republican Party

**Happy Independence Day!** On this day in 1845, a convention assembled in Austin to consider the congressional resolution proposing the annexation of the Republic of Texas to the United States. The delegates [accepted the proposal](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJyk0DGOqzAQgOHTmA40HgyEwsVr6PLaLZGJB2zF8URmFCe3X-1eYS_w_9L3dV2vLqaYj__uQVbeO6-Z6plIhMoaWAKn6N2nEt0p-8yl0hHdioBjC1MLZvUups9qGm838LNuyOrp0uuxB8AmWJhxgNmgm2Y9EO43jdrMqE2_Qz-YuYn2JwYTGK2hR90B-MmMI_ptRDNdNmWAfBQunQQSertzTx9-Uelu_GiSDSLPU_X_FC4Kl1prJ2dwnFPM1HE5FC7BZb8x3xUulKVEOhUuN84vyhI5t7y3-mKGplj_rDGleI6TMnA8XEy_F_mbzcvidwAAAP__c5Z3lw) by a vote of 55-1. As our nation commemorates its 250th birthday this weekend, we'll be sending out shortened editions through Monday, so _The Texas Flyover _staff can celebrate the holiday with friends and family. Our regular edition will return on Tuesday. Have a safe and happy Fourth of July weekend!

Are you the one setting off fireworks, or the one lying awake wishing they'd stop? Somewhere on your street tonight, someone's going till midnight while the dog shakes under the bed and half the block wonders if they're the only ones who've had enough. Fireworks are the sound of the Fourth, the whole country looking up at once. But they're also sparking wildfire fears, veterans bracing at every crack, and thousands of ER visits a year. Friends,

Yesterday I had the privilege of joining Fox News live from Independence Hall in Philadelphia, the cradle of American democracy, to talk about why the next generation of Americans inspires me.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fq6MoT8yYsQ [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fq6MoT8yYsQ]

Keep up the fire. 🇺🇸

I've told this story before, but with many thousands of new subscribers, it's worth telling again, particularly today. If you missed it before, it's about everything America could and should be for the world. And what we stand to lose if we aren't that country anymore.
Lucas's Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9sdWNhc2t1bmNlLnN1YnN0YWNrLmNvbS9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.3cwGvX8PhU2i6Uuz36MkOlp78VkC1S5A_0o-yYxGpdM?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget-preamble&utm_content=205041900)
Growing up, my mom had to get creative looking for cheap or free ways to keep us kids entertained during the summers. The standard strategy included: swimming lessons at the public pool, long hours at the public library, and attending every single vacation bible school in town.
And when I say every single one, I mean... Every. Single. One. Catholic, Lutheran, Episcopalian, Disciples of Christ, Southern Baptist, you name it...
You'd think this diversity of faiths and locations would have kept things interesting. However, the truth is that you did basically the same thing at all of them. The same coloring sheets. The same songs. The same parachute games. The same ten stories.
Once a summer, however, we got to do something special. Lincoln University, right down the street from our house, hosted a program called Learning Unlimited, where you got to do all sorts of cool stuff. Write plays, make pottery, cook exotic food, play red rover, learn integers.
Well, ok, maybe it wasn't ALL cool, but it sure beat coloring in a cutout of Daniel in the Lion's Den and pasting it onto a popsicle stick for the tenth week in a row.
Learning Unlimited is also where I first met my friend for life and future best man, Benyam (whose Washington Post op-ed about running black in America I [featured in a previous substack](https://substack.com/redirect/68812080-9aad-4bca-8340-84ac56a7416d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)). His parents, refugees of the Eritrean war of Independence against Ethiopia, were drawn to mid-Missouri because they had family here and because Lincoln University, as an HBCU, was a welcoming environment for them. Benyam's mom graduated from Lincoln and his parents worked there until their retirement.
In all the years growing up learning how to eat injera and dance like a habesha at his house, Benyam's dad was quietly in the background. Always supportive and entirely encouraging, sometimes funny, but never standing out in any way. Certainly not as your macho-masculine tough guy.
To be real about it, Benyam's mom, Turu, seemed like the badass of the house. I mean, she smashed spiders with her bare feet and ate ground beef raw out of the package! The hardest thing we ever saw Benyam's old man do was gargle rubbing alcohol. Which is admittedly pretty fierce, but not exactly worth any street cred with the other kids. And the most interesting thing about the collected old man was probably that his toes were kind of crooked.
Well, that or maybe his weird name: Tesfai (which is pronounced tess-fi, with the fi like the fi in wifi).
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/32d8d86d-d957-4a52-9bb4-4166eb5795e9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Turu and Tesfai
Benyam and I are still friends, and a few years ago, when I was stationed at the Pentagon, Benyam called me upset. One of his uncles had gotten agitated at a family gathering and told Benyam that a man who had tortured his dad years ago in the home country was now a cab driver here in the US.
Tortured?! I asked, incredulous.
Yeah, man, it's nuts. I had no idea, said Benyam. Absolutely crazy. Apparently Pops was thrown in a black hole and nearly tortured to death for who knows how long back in the day. And now we know that the guy who did it is here, just living the good life, like it's nothing. I can't just sit here. I gotta go after this guy. Expose him. He's a damn war criminal. I've at least gotta confront him. How can I be a man knowing that this guy is out there just living free in America after what he's done?
Benyam obsessed over the idea of confronting the man who had tortured his father. He dug into whatever details he could find. He interrogated relatives in pursuit of more information on what had happened. He talked to just about everyone he could. Well except, his dad, of course.
Time went by. Benyam and I mulled over ways to approach the man who had tortured Tesfai. Get into his cab. Ambush him on a podcast. Report him as a war criminal. But first we needed to know more.
Then, in 2021, we were at Benyam's parents' house in Jefferson City for the Fourth of July. Sitting in their living room, with Benyam's two little girls and his parents, someone asked Benyam's parents to tell us how they came to America, thinking it would be a fun all-American immigration story for the Fourth.
His parents talked about growing up in then-Ethiopia in the 50's and 60's. Benyam's mom showed us a picture of her being honored by the Emperor of Ethiopia at her high school graduation and another photo of Tesfai with a live lion. She talked about how her family and Tesfai, who she was only dating at the time, had encouraged her to escape seek a better life during the wars. How a relative of Tesfai's in Missouri had eventually gotten Turu to Jefferson City, where she attended Lincoln and worked at the Hotel DeVille's restaurant to make ends meet. At the time, Tesfai worked for Ethiopian Airlines, and was able to get to Kansas City through work, so they could still occasionally see each other.
Ultimately, as the conflict in Eritrea intensified, Tesfai decided to give up his job and come to America to be with Turu. But he needed to take one last trip back to Eritrea to get everything in order. It was a classic love story intertwined with the American Dream. From the way they spoke, you could feel the light that America held for the rest of the world during those years.
Back home, however, the story took a dark turn. Before Tesfai could depart, he was snatched for questioning by local police. If not for a family member seeing it happen, he would have simply disappeared and no one would have known.
As Tesfai spoke, Benyam was riveted to his seat. This is what he had been wanting to hear for years but never knew how to ask for. He wanted all the details. We quietly bribed his little girls to go to the other room with their tablets while Tesfai continued.
It was a common story in Eritrean Ethiopia at the time. Tesfai had just been unlucky. In the wrong place at the wrong time.
He was taken into captivity and accused of political crimes he didn't even know had happened and wasn't in the country to commit. They accused him of being a revolutionary. They locked him away, hidden from the world, and without communication. They tortured him to get a confession. He described some of the terrible things they did. One relentless man in particular. We learned how he had gotten his crooked toes. We heard what it was like to break, to get to the point where you would say anything or do anything to make the pain stop.
Turu talked about how her dreams disappeared when Tesfai did. About what it was like, being in America, such a safe place, surrounded by prosperity, while Tesfai was locked away. She didn't know what he was going through, she wouldn't have even known why he hadn't come and why he wasn't writing her if that relative hadn't been lucky enough to see him taken and let everyone know. She talked about how overwhelming it was not knowing if he was alive or dead, or if she would ever know.
One day, Tesfai said, nearly a year later, he was simply set free. With no explanation, no direction, no nothing. Just dumped back on the street. He made his way back to family and tried to put his life back together.
From then on, everywhere he went he was terrified. Looking over his shoulder, waiting to be taken again. Travel out of the country was restricted, yet his old boss at the airline secured him a flight to America, an incredibly risky thing for him to do. Tesfai couldn't leave, however, unless someone was willing to sign an attestation and vouch that he would return. He couldn't ask someone to do that, because he knew what would happen to them when he didn't come back.
An older gentleman, barely an acquaintance, a friend of a friend, heard about Tesfai's plight when they were all at a bar commiserating about what life had become. The old man approached Tesfai and calmly and simply told him that he would vouch for him.
Tesfai, in shock, refused. He couldn't put this man at risk. But the man, who was ready to risk his life for a stranger and a love story, insisted. Tesfai asked him to sleep on it.
The next day the man signed the papers.
Tesfai was too afraid to call Turu and tell her, in case someone was listening. His anxiety grew as the day of his flight came closer. Tesfai had second thoughts. Perhaps it was a set-up and the man was a government agent. But Tesfai wouldn't have another chance and, as he had learned, danger lurked around every corner.
When the day arrived, Tesfai made his way to the airport. He was sure he wouldn't make it onto the plane and expected that tap on his shoulder at any moment. In his mind, every sound was the sound of armed guards pushing through the crowd to carry him off. Once airborne, every shift in the sky was the plane turning back to take him back in. The delay during his connection was because security was coming to grab him.
But, then, just like that, he landed in America. And he was free.
The rest, as they say, is history. His grandchildren were called back into the room. Benyam's parents told us about re-uniting, marrying, and having their two boys. How they raised them as Missourians, and worked full productive careers in America before finally retiring a few years ago.
Benyam was speechless. This was his moment to dig, but he was frozen. I stepped in and told Tesfai what we had heard. That the man who tortured him was living in America. That he would likely never answer for what he had done. I asked him what he thought about that.
Tesfai looked at us like we were two schoolchildren.
"Let him have peace," Tesfai said calmly and without hesitation. "I made peace with it a long time ago. If I had chosen hate, or resentment, or dwelled on what he had done, it would have ruined this beautiful life we made here in America. I would have lost even more than he had taken. Jesus showed us the power to forgive. I follow his example."
He took Turu's hand and they smiled at us, the sound of their grandchildren playing in the background, gearing up to watch the fireworks over the Missouri River that night and celebrate 245 years of American freedom with their grandpa, an American hero.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/57a99500-63b1-4085-a5c3-9ba57a7d0ae0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
With an American Hero on a campaign shoot
Happy Fourth of July,
Lucas

clean_body: I've told this story before, but with many thousands of new subscribers, it's worth telling again, particularly today. | | ---|---|--- | | | Forwarded this email? ? for more ? | | | Jul 4 | | | | | | | | | | | | I've told this story before, but with many thousands of new subscribers, it's worth telling again, particularly today. If you missed it before, it's about everything America could and should be for the world. And what we stand to lose if we aren't that country anymore. Lucas's Substack is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. Growing up, my mom had to get creative looking for cheap or free ways to keep us kids entertained during the summers. The standard strategy included: swimming lessons at the public pool, long hours at the public library, and attending every single vacation bible school in town. And when I say every single one, I mean... Every. Single. One. Catholic, Lutheran, Episcopalian, Disciples of Christ, Southern Baptist, you name it... You'd think this diversity of faiths and locations would have kept things interesting. However, the truth is that you did basically the same thing at all of them. The same coloring sheets. The same songs. The same parachute games. The same ten stories. Once a summer, however, we got to do something special. Lincoln University, right down the street from our house, hosted a program called Learning Unlimited, where you got to do all sorts of cool stuff. Write plays, make pottery, cook exotic food, play red rover, learn integers. Well, ok, maybe it wasn't ALL cool, but it sure beat coloring in a cutout of Daniel in the Lion's Den and pasting it onto a popsicle stick for the tenth week in a row. Learning Unlimited is also where I first met my friend for life and future best man, Benyam (whose Washington Post op-ed about running black in America I ). His parents, refugees of the Eritrean war of Independence against Ethiopia, were drawn to mid-Missouri because they had family here and because Lincoln University, as an HBCU, was a welcoming environment for them. Benyam's mom graduated from Lincoln and his parents worked there until their retirement. In all the years growing up learning how to eat injera and dance like a habesha at his house, Benyam's dad was quietly in the background. Always supportive and entirely encouraging, sometimes funny, but never standing out in any way. Certainly not as your macho-masculine tough guy. To be real about it, Benyam's mom, Turu, seemed like the badass of the house. I mean, she smashed spiders with her bare feet and ate ground beef raw out of the package! The hardest thing we ever saw Benyam's old man do was gargle rubbing alcohol. Which is admittedly pretty fierce, but not exactly worth any street cred with the other kids. And the most interesting thing about the collected old man was probably that his toes were kind of crooked. Well, that or maybe his weird name: Tesfai (which is pronounced tess-fi, with the fi like the fi in wifi). | | ---|---|--- Turu and Tesfai Benyam and I are still friends, and a few years ago, when I was stationed at the Pentagon, Benyam called me upset. One of his uncles had gotten agitated at a family gathering and told Benyam that a man who had tortured his dad years ago in the home country was now a cab driver here in the US. Tortured?! I asked, incredulous. Yeah, man, it's nuts. I had no idea, said Benyam. Absolutely crazy. Apparently Pops was thrown in a black hole and nearly tortured to death for who knows how long back in the day. And now we know that the guy who did it is here, just living the good life, like it's nothing. I can't just sit here. I gotta go after this guy. Expose him. He's a damn war criminal. I've at least gotta confront him. How can I be a man knowing that this guy is out there just living free in America after what he's done? Benyam obsessed over the idea of confronting the man who had tortured his father. He dug into whatever details he could find. He interrogated relatives in pursuit of more information on what had happened. He talked to just about everyone he could. Well except, his dad, of course. Time went by. Benyam and I mulled over ways to approach the man who had tortured Tesfai. Get into his cab. Ambush him on a podcast. Report him as a war criminal. But first we needed to know more. Then, in 2021, we were at Benyam's parents' house in Jefferson City for the Fourth of July. Sitting in their living room, with Benyam's two little girls and his parents, someone asked Benyam's parents to tell us how they came to America, thinking it would be a fun all-American immigration story for the Fourth. His parents talked about growing up in then-Ethiopia in the 50's and 60's. Benyam's mom showed us a picture of her being honored by the Emperor of Ethiopia at her high school graduation and another photo of Tesfai with a live lion. She talked about how her family and Tesfai, who she was only dating at the time, had encouraged her to escape seek a better life during the wars. How a relative of Tesfai's in Missouri had eventually gotten Turu to Jefferson City, where she attended Lincoln and worked at the Hotel DeVille's restaurant to make ends meet. At the time, Tesfai worked for Ethiopian Airlines, and was able to get to Kansas City through work, so they could still occasionally see each other. Ultimately, as the conflict in Eritrea intensified, Tesfai decided to give up his job and come to America to be with Turu. But he needed to take one last trip back to Eritrea to get everything in order. It was a classic love story intertwined with the American Dream. From the way they spoke, you could feel the light that America held for the rest of the world during those years. Back home, however, the story took a dark turn. Before Tesfai could depart, he was snatched for questioning by local police. If not for a family member seeing it happen, he would have simply disappeared and no one would have known. As Tesfai spoke, Benyam was riveted to his seat. This is what he had been wanting to hear for years but never knew how to ask for. He wanted all the details. We quietly bribed his little girls to go to the other room with their tablets while Tesfai continued. It was a common story in Eritrean Ethiopia at the time. Tesfai had just been unlucky. In the wrong place at the wrong time. He was taken into captivity and accused of political crimes he didn't even know had happened and wasn't in the country to commit. They accused him of being a revolutionary. They locked him away, hidden from the world, and without communication. They tortured him to get a confession. He described some of the terrible things they did. One relentless man in particular. We learned how he had gotten his crooked toes. We heard what it was like to break, to get to the point where you would say anything or do anything to make the pain stop. Turu talked about how her dreams disappeared when Tesfai did. About what it was like, being in America, such a safe place, surrounded by prosperity, while Tesfai was locked away. She didn't know what he was going through, she wouldn't have even known why he hadn't come and why he wasn't writing her if that relative hadn't been lucky enough to see him taken and let everyone know. She talked about how overwhelming it was not knowing if he was alive or dead, or if she would ever know. One day, Tesfai said, nearly a year later, he was simply set free. With no explanation, no direction, no nothing. Just dumped back on the street. He made his way back to family and tried to put his life back together. From then on, everywhere he went he was terrified. Looking over his shoulder, waiting to be taken again. Travel out of the country was restricted, yet his old boss at the airline secured him a flight to America, an incredibly risky thing for him to do. Tesfai couldn't leave, however, unless someone was willing to sign an attestation and vouch that he would return. He couldn't ask someone to do that, because he knew what would happen to them when he didn't come back. An older gentleman, barely an acquaintance, a friend of a friend, heard about Tesfai's plight when they were all at a bar commiserating about what life had become. The old man approached Tesfai and calmly and simply told him that he would vouch for him. Tesfai, in shock, refused. He couldn't put this man at risk. But the man, who was ready to risk his life for a stranger and a love story, insisted. Tesfai asked him to sleep on it. The next day the man signed the papers. Tesfai was too afraid to call Turu and tell her, in case someone was listening. His anxiety grew as the day of his flight came closer. Tesfai had second thoughts. Perhaps it was a set-up and the man was a government agent. But Tesfai wouldn't have another chance and, as he had learned, danger lurked around every corner. When the day arrived, Tesfai made his way to the airport. He was sure he wouldn't make it onto the plane and expected that tap on his shoulder at any moment. In his mind, every sound was the sound of armed guards pushing through the crowd to carry him off. Once airborne, every shift in the sky was the plane turning back to take him back in. The delay during his connection was because security was coming to grab him. But, then, just like that, he landed in America. And he was free. The rest, as they say, is history. His grandchildren were called back into the room. Benyam's parents told us about re-uniting, marrying, and having their two boys. How they raised them as Missourians, and worked full productive careers in America before finally retiring a few years ago. Benyam was speechless. This was his moment to dig, but he was frozen. I stepped in and told Tesfai what we had heard. That the man who tortured him was living in America. That he would likely never answer for what he had done. I asked him what he thought about that. Tesfai looked at us like we were two schoolchildren. "Let him have peace," Tesfai said calmly and without hesitation. "I made peace with it a long time ago. If I had chosen hate, or resentment, or dwelled on what he had done, it would have ruined this beautiful life we made here in America. I would have lost even more than he had taken. Jesus showed us the power to forgive. I follow his example." He took Turu's hand and they smiled at us, the sound of their grandchildren playing in the background, gearing up to watch the fireworks over the Missouri River that night and celebrate 245 years of American freedom with their grandpa, an American hero. | | ---|---|--- With an American Hero on a campaign shoot Happy Fourth of July, Lucas Lucas's Substack is a reader-supported publication. Peter, As we celebrate Independence Day, I’ve been reflecting on what it means to be an American.

Yes, our politics have become too toxic, and too much of what we see coming out of Washington can make it feel like we are losing our sense of honor, compassion and common purpose. But away from the Washington circus, I still see the best of America every day. I see it when someone holds a door open, lets another driver go ahead, checks on a neighbor, volunteers in the community or helps a person in need.

That is where America’s real strength has always been. It is found in each of us, and in the choices we make every day to lift one another up.

That spirit is especially important as we celebrate the Fourth of July and mark America’s 250th birthday, a moment to reflect on our history, our challenges and the opportunity for hope. [I recently wrote a column about how we can renew the promise of this country](http://links.johnkasich.com/s/c/9TkjtTA-CbSS7PcKZoJ3sWRvHIWX_HWhCpWoE5tsT22N_9IfBr_Vt8mRYqHVfkWE5oxTbV5UbRQ0ZHkAcMl4vsJF9tZBq7AgUKPYVMWdD_pnWyV78YLCTMAWXRDVqHJUI8B6hbeLE8uD1P_k0RC_3Uj1ryddtQmMFlzgZMgUrErXKt7g-n20NV9Pluj0d0F7mXkr1mSeMY3a94HFvvROHWnaEzug-R_oJyoHEuMfdmL_JqluWWCxAxj0FH7YQeXUMswl3fSKsNCdMGL2aQ1W00sP_fCCQzA-htnARtWvQJXLBJexCzOzLmSxYWb9WSj7slmO5_UWFI2Ro0icL-pSYy01ly-wcTMdsSBRbuZ1nJysy6-7-qK1HAjtsS0sZH87bocv2MMUDkxYX5BZ6gsENmtfBthErobPbtcU6vT9OAgfXvkCkX91XyEf4P4avZ_EkVgCEv9rNWYrGvScmEhOWgNVPg/dnGJwfrDf6DGvLxNAdE5j9BNWkBfBi8k/22), not only through our leaders, but through our families, neighborhoods, houses of worship, charities and communities.

name: Douglas Carswell
subject: America is the Indispensable Country
body:
| | | [View this email in your browser](https://mailchi.mp/mspolicy/july4th?e=5703353baa)
---
| |
---
| _**If you're not in front of our Saturday email, you're behind.**_
---
| Dear Friend,
Imagine if there had never been a Declaration of Independence. There are, after all, plenty of places once ruled by Britain — Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, Belize — that gradually acquired their independence over time. What if the thirteen colonies had done the same: not broken with the motherland, but gradually drifted from her, becoming a collection of Canadas? Some historians think that, had George III possessed a different temperament, that is almost certainly what would have happened. Instead of a Congress and a President, we might have a parliament and a prime minister, as they do in Ottawa. Thank goodness America did declare independence. Had she not, the world would be a much worse place. It's not that I have anything against Canada, or Australia — or indeed my own country, Britain. It's that the moment Jefferson and co asserted the supremacy of natural rights over pre-modern claims of authority, the American model was born. The United States was conceived in the Declaration of Independence, delivered at the Constitutional Convention in 1787, and grew to become the pinnacle of human achievement. The Declaration was the essential moment — the assertion that natural rights come first, and that power flows from We the People. The longer I live in America, the more I appreciate being here — and the more I realize just how precious and distinctive this country really is. America is the indispensable country. Founded 250 years ago on a document proclaiming the right to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, today she underwrites those things across much of the planet.
---
|
---
_Celebrate July 4th..._
| We all know about Elon Musk — a titanic figure of our times, who has built one world-changing technology and industry after another. He is part pioneering engineer in the mold of Nikola Tesla, part businessman in the mold of Vanderbilt, and part hero of liberty in the mold of John Wilkes. But stop and ask a basic question: could Elon have done any of it had he stayed in one of the countries he passed through before he came to America? Had Musk remained in South Africa, or Canada — or, heaven forbid, moved to Europe — would he have achieved a single one of his achievements? You only have to ask the question to see the genius of America. The laws of physics are no different here; nor is the air, or the water. It is what Jefferson and co set in motion with their signatures 250 years ago today. My only regret about America declaring her independence from Britain? That I missed so much of the first 245 years, having moved here only five years ago.
---

---
| |
---
Warm regards,

Douglas Carswell
President & CEO
Mississippi Center for Public Policy

name: Stacy Garrity
subject: 250 Years of Freedom
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Garrity for PA[View email in browser](https://mailchi
body:
Today, our nation celebrates an extraordinary milestone.

| | | | | |
---
| | | | | | Peter,
Today, our nation celebrates an extraordinary milestone.
For 250 years, the United States of America has stood as the world's greatest force for freedom, hope, and opportunity. Ours is the story of ordinary people accomplishing extraordinary things—a nation founded on the revolutionary idea that our rights come not from government, but from God.
That promise has been preserved by generations of Americans willing to defend it.
Think of the farmers who left their fields to fight for independence. Think of the soldiers who endured Valley Forge, preserved our Union at Gettysburg, stormed the beaches of Normandy, answered the call after September 11th, and continue to wear our nation's uniform today.
They came from different places and different generations, but they shared one conviction:
**America is worth serving.**
I know what it means to answer that call.
Serving our country for 30 years in the United States Army Reserve remains one of the greatest privileges of my life. I served alongside Americans from every walk of life, united by a love of country and a commitment to something greater than themselves. In uniform, you learn that freedom isn't an abstract idea. It has a cost, and every generation has been blessed with Americans willing to pay it.
That's why Independence Day means so much to me.
As you celebrate with family, friends, food, and fireworks today, I hope you'll pause for a moment.
Remember the young Continental soldier who could never have imagined what America would become. Remember every service member who stood a lonely watch so families here at home could gather in freedom. And remember that the flag flying over your home is more than a symbol of our history—it is a promise to our future.
Two hundred fifty years later, America remains the greatest experiment in self-government the world has ever known.
It is still worth believing in.
It is still worth protecting.
It is still worth serving.
---

body:

| | | | | [|

| |
# _Happy 250th Independence Day!_
---
| | _This week, we celebrate something extraordinary: 250 years of American independence._
---
|
---
| | | | | |
As I've reflected on what this milestone means for southern Indiana, I keep coming back to the people who've quietly built this country for generations — the families who've farmed the same land for over a century, the workers who've quarried limestone in Bedford that helped build the U.S. Capitol, the Pentagon, the Empire State Building, and countless courthouses and churches across America.
That's the story of our district, and it's the story of America.
Recently, I had the honor of contributing to Congress's America 250 Time Capsule, set to be opened on our nation's 500th birthday in 2276. I chose a piece of Indiana limestone, a small reminder that America's greatest landmarks weren't built by Washington alone. They were built by skilled hands in communities like ours.
**This week also marks one year since President Trump signed the Working Families Tax Cuts Act into law** — and the results speak for themselves:
* The largest tax refund season in American history, with the average refund topping $3,400.
* Nearly 20 million Americans claimed no tax on overtime.
* Over 6 million claimed no tax on tips.
* An overwhelming majority of seniors paid no tax on Social Security income.
* Nearly 12 million small business owners saw an average tax cut of almost $7,000.
* Family farms protected from a higher death tax, so the next generation doesn't have to sell the farm to keep it.

These aren't just numbers. They are parents with more breathing room in the family budget. They are small business owners hiring another employee. They are farmers planning for the future instead of worrying if their legacy survives.
Our founders believed hard work should be rewarded and every generation has a duty to leave this country stronger than they found it. 250 years later, that promise still holds, and it's one worth fighting for. Thank you for being part of this story.
With Gratitude,Erin Houchin

subject: 250 years of freedom. Let's fight for 250 more.

body:
The Founders didn't defeat one tyranny to hand us another. Here's what we owe them.

| | | | | [|
---](https://ericburlisonforcongress.us5.list-manage.com/track/click?u=b6500a115da3c4344522b1e48&id=4b306ca924&e=5f9dc01b8c)
| | Peter ,
Two hundred and fifty years ago, ordinary Americans did something extraordinary. Farmers, blacksmiths, and shopkeepers picked up muskets and stood against the most powerful empire on earth. They pledged their lives, their fortunes, and their sacred honor, and many of them paid in full.
They did it for one reason. Freedom.
They did not defeat one tyranny just to build another, one that buries our kids in debt, tries to control your medicine, register your firearms, and tell you what you can put on your own dinner table. That is not the country they built. They gave us a limited government, and it is our job to keep it that way.
[](https://ericburlisonforcongress.us5.list-manage.com/track/click?u=b6500a115da3c4344522b1e48&id=32de45f106&e=5f9dc01b8c)

body:
Too many have yet to see the equality and justice that the 4th of July represents.

[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/134595289/631639793/-153530995?refcode=EM_C_260704fourth_N_SB_30DO_4_NG_N_Logo&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMjEvMS84Nzg0NCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICIyMWFkZmYzZi1hODc3LWYxMTEtYWM5Yy0wMDBkM2ExNGI2ZDYiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=t19TPMRPrBpRXa7X8GZdD2SMdCyXd5c_g-oiKKJgIuM=) Peter,

Today, Americans across the country will gather in celebration of 250 years of independence – to share community and to embrace those we hold dear. As we gather around the grills, swimming pools, and fireworks, I wanted to take a moment to reflect on what Independence Day means for us all.

**The truth is that, despite 250 years of fighting to ensure our nation works for everyone, too many have yet to see the equality and justice that the 4th of July represents.** In fact, this week also marks the one-year anniversary of the GOP’s Big Ugly Bill, making the largest cuts to Medicaid in our nation’s history, ripping healthcare away from 17 million Americans, slashing food assistance, and making college more expensive for working families – all to fund massive tax cuts for the wealthiest Americans. Working families are paying more for groceries, housing, utilities, and prescription drugs, while the Trump administration is focused on building ballrooms, renovating fountains, and attacking our elections.

The Trump administration and House Republicans are doing everything in their power to strip away our rights, stall progress, and take our nation backward. We can’t and won’t let that happen. With you by our side, we must fight to take back the House and fight for the future of our great nation.

I hope we all take today to reflect on not only our independence but that of every American, no matter their background, color, or creed. We have a major fight ahead of us this November, but together, I know we can create the equality and justice we need for all.

Onward,

Shontel Brown | Shontel Brown is proud to be elected as the Congresswoman for Ohio’s 11th District. She has spent the last decade serving the people of Ohio and building coalitions. As she enters her second full term in Congress, she will use that experience to continue the fight for affordable quality health care, jobs that pay fair wages, a strong public education system, and to preserve and protect our democracy for generations to come. Will you join her and be the change we need?

body:
A review of Vikram's June posts...

| | | | | | | [View this email in your browser](https://mailchi.mp/mansharamani/vikram-update-june-17450340?e=93b2c2b824)
---
[|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/192Am64xQRE?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586)
| | | | | |
# Mansharamani Musings
---
| | [](https://us.list-manage.com/GXrWDUaPPXe?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586)From the Iran War to domestic primary elections and from AI’s continued march forward to the kick-off of the World Cup in the United States, June has been a month filled with attention grabbing headlines. As regular readers are aware, my weekly posts are drafted to shed light on topics that I don’t think are getting adequate attention and yet may help you navigate uncertainty. It was in that spirit that my four most recent pieces address the forthcoming boom in fiber, the intensification of geopolitical rivalry in the Arctic, a teenager’s take on how to generate a more peaceful world, and the impact of demographics on education, retirement, and our economy as a whole. I welcome feedback. Best wishes for a thought-filled July! Happy Birthday America!_**
- Vikram**_

---
[|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/6JE4Xg9b6j8?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586)
| | **June 7, 2026**

The protein boom is alive and well. Unless you live under a rock, you’ve likely seen protein being marketed on almost every food item you buy. [Doritos](https://us.list-manage.com/MjqNOyGuKnD?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586), your [coffee](https://us.list-manage.com/AYPYxvLIOIW?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586), and even your [ice cream](https://us.list-manage.com/poYV7herOC4?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586) now trumpet their protein content. And it’s not just a marketing story; consumers are demanding more protein. [A majority of Americans](https://us.list-manage.com/13sWQ0To_eK?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586) say they’re actively trying to eat more of it. Meat snacks alone have become a [$5.5 billion juggernaut](https://us.list-manage.com/J1abJS_ivCF?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586), and #protein[ has millions of posts on Instagram, TikTok and YouTube](https://us.list-manage.com/gxhM1xgVZNh?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586). These days, the word “protein” on a package is almost as important as the price.
Food fads are not new, and while I believe the protein story isn’t a fleeting phenomenon, it’s not unreasonable to question the sustainability of the boom. After all, before protein, American consumers were infatuated with hydration. Remember when Liquid I.V. suddenly appeared everywhere? When everyone started carrying water bottles and Stanley cups became a status symbol?
It seems to me there’s a pattern here. First, a real health concept goes mainstream, social media amplifies interest in the topic, the food industry builds an empire with brands and products to help consumers achieve their goals, our culture changes to incorporate the new desires, and suddenly it’s in every aisle of your grocery store...
---
| [CLICK HERE TO CONTINUE READING](https://us.list-manage.com/UQXV8D09ROB?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586)
---
|
---
[|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/19j5k8Sixtf?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586)
| | **June 14, 2026**

History may not repeat itself, but it often does rhyme. As resources become valuable, major powers scramble to secure access to them. But it’s not just the resources that matter, it’s the ability to get (to) them; inevitably, chokepoints emerge, and great powers start jockeying for position. In many cases, success in securing materials or trade routes is enough to reorient global power dynamics.
Rome conquered the Mediterranean in the 2nd century BC because it meant control of trade. For a thousand years (or so), the Silk Road drove empires from the Han Dynasty to the Mongols to battle for control of Central Asian corridors. The spice trade led the Portuguese and the Dutch into conflict over nutmeg in the 1500s and 1600s. The 1908 discovery of oil in Persia redrew the map of the Middle East, and we’re still fighting over those lines today. And Britain and Russia spent the entire 19th century playing what [Kipling called the “Great Game” across Central Asia, with India as the grand prize](https://us.list-manage.com/JjpHnv_1ycO?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586). Battles over resources and trading routes is nothing new.

Today, another Great Game is underway in the north. As I have written before, I believe the next couple of decades will see a Great Power contest for the Arctic, and it is already heating up....
---

[|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/sWT3MLk0x8C?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586)
| | **June 21, 2026**

Last weekend, my family headed north to watch my 15-year-old son Kai deliver a speech to the Rotary Club in Orford, Quebec. As someone who has been a professional speaker for more than 15 years, I was genuinely impressed by both his message and delivery. I could not have been more proud.
I hope you’ll indulge me on this Father’s Day and take 6 minutes to watch (or at least listen to) his speech. Yes, I’m a proud father who wants to brag about his son. But I’m also a concerned citizen and want his powerful message of hope and optimism to be shared and spread as widely as possible. He offers a path towards a more compassionate and peaceful politics.
And if you like his speech, please consider [subscribing to his podcast, The Kai Guy Show, on Apple Podcasts](https://us.list-manage.com/jbw8qDCWm8f?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586) where he regularly shares his thoughts. Please also consider sharing his speech via the share button below with family, friends, and colleagues.
---
| [CLICK HERE TO CONTINUE READING](https://us.list-manage.com/ZOsqtBXRJEl?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586)

[|
---](https://us.list-manage.com/hgWjIW3DYmF?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586)
| | **May 24, 2026**

[4,316,233 babies were born in the United States](https://us.list-manage.com/c0qLhbYnmSE?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586) during 2007, the most in American history. The fertility rate, a measure of how many children are born per woman, stood at 2.12, almost exactly at the level needed to keep the population stable.
All of that seemed to change in 2008. When Lehman Brothers collapsed on September 15, 2008, the birth rate collapsed along with it. The number of births in America had already started slipping earlier in 2008 (~68,000 fewer babies than the year before) but by 2009, births had [dropped to 4,131,000](https://us.list-manage.com/2ZUVuNWA39x?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586) (~185,000 below the 2007 peak.) And it just kept falling. Through the recovery, through the bull market, through the lowest unemployment in half a century. Year after year after year.
Last year, [3.6 million babies were born](https://us.list-manage.com/HjFXcs8fNRl?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586); that’s **700,000 fewer than the 2007 peak**. The fertility rate hit [another record low: 1.6 children per woman](https://us.list-manage.com/t5kLUZkWadz?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586), well below the replacement rate, and government demographers believe it will stay near 1.6 [through 2055](https://us.list-manage.com/h9QmFrejPfs?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586)....

| | **VIKRAM MANSHARAMANI** is an entrepreneur, consultant, scholar, neighbor, husband, father, volunteer, and professional generalist who thinks in multiple-dimensions and looks beyond the short-term. Self-taught to think around corners and connect original dots, he spends his time speaking with global leaders in business, government, academia, and journalism. **He’s currently the Chairman and CEO of Goodwell Foods, a manufacturer of private label frozen pizza**. _LinkedIn_ has twice listed him as its #1 Top Voice in Money & Finance, and _Worth_ profiled him as one of the 100 Most Powerful People in Global Finance. Vikram earned a PhD From MIT, has taught at Yale and Harvard, and is the author of three books, [ _**The Making of a Generalist: An Independent Thinker Finds Unconventional Success in an Uncertain World**_](https://us.list-manage.com/yQBowSCUqsu?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586) , [ _**Think for Yourself: Restoring Common Sense in an Age of Experts and Artificial Intelligence**_](https://us.list-manage.com/2aGPONUsGOd?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586) and [ _**Boombustology: Spotting Financial Bubbles Before They Burst**_](https://us.list-manage.com/983dJgzKzss?e=93b2c2b824&c2id=8d3705edc40ffd26940a732b7f12f586). body:
# [](https://act.betoorourke.com/go/43706?t=1&akid=240939%2E444211%2EoHO2zZ)
I'm spending the 4th with family, going to a friend's 51st birthday party ("don't let the old man in!" is the advice I've been given and will in turn share about getting older) and taking some time to reflect on our good fortune.
These are tough days, dark ones for our country. Never since the Civil War have we had such an existential threat to our freedoms, our Constitution, and the founding American idea that we are all created equal and should be treated so under the law. The consolidation of authoritarian power in the hands of our current President, the corruption committed in broad daylight, the cruelty that is a feature of this regime... it can tempt us to despair.
But let's remember that we've been through darker, tougher times before. 250 years ago we took on the most powerful empire on the planet to ensure that no American would ever bow to a king again. A few generations later we decided that no American could ever claim ownership over another by defeating the armies of the Confederacy at the cost of more than 360,000 Union soldiers killed. We took on the Nazis in World War II, Americans giving their lives to stop fascism abroad and protect democracy at home. And not even a generation after that, brave civil and voting rights activists overcame the overwhelming power of Jim Crow (harassment, imprisonment and murder) and forced this country to reckon with the idea of equality in practice, producing the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
We've been up against some tough, long odds since 1776. And though it has never been easy, and though it has come at great cost to those Americans willing to put their lives on the line for this country and the ideals it represents, we have always come through.
Remember that and remember that there are a lot of good people out there right now. Candidates putting their names on the ballot, activists putting their lives on the line (Minneapolis and beyond), advocates and volunteers giving their time and talent, good people of good conscience doing what they can with what they have wherever they are.
We are going to come through these challenges like we've come through them before... working together, across and despite our differences, having the courage the moment demands, willing to sacrifice and doing the work that is going to make the difference.
We'll emerge from this trial closer to realizing our promise and potential, inspiring the generations to come just as those before have inspired us.
Happy Independence Day,
Beto

body:
Today, celebrate the United States of America. The oldest representative democracy in the entire world. As Lincoln called it, “the last best hope of earth.”
#
Peter, happy Independence Day.
250 years ago today, American democracy was born. In spite of everything that’s happened, that democracy endures today. Whether it survives for the next generation is up to us.
Do not let Donald Trump take this day from you. It belongs to every American who grew up saying the Pledge of Allegiance in school — and everyone who didn’t, too. To every Veteran and every civilian. Every Democrat, every Republican, and every independent. No matter your religion, where your family came from, or who you love. It’s yours.
If you believe in democracy — the simple and radical idea that each of us have equal rights, equality before the law, and an equal say in our future — this is your day. And if you really do believe that, we hope you’re willing to fight for it.
There are countless flashpoints in American history where the flame of our democracy could have been snuffed out. Over the years, patriots met those moments with enough courage and resolve to keep it alight. They got us this far.
Today, celebrate the United States of America. The oldest representative democracy in the entire world. As Lincoln called it, “the last best hope of earth.”
Tomorrow, get out there and fight for it.
Thank you.
The team at VoteVets

| | | Dear Parents,Looking for a screen-free activity that's fun, educational, and bursting with star-spangled pride?

Introducing Color Across America—the coloring book that brings 250 years of American history to life, one crayon stroke at a time! Your child will discover:* The Founding Fathers and the birth of our nation* The Liberty Bell and the Statue of Liberty * American heroes and historic landmarks* Space exploration, innovation, and amazing inventions* The values of freedom, courage, and opportunityEvery page is designed to spark curiosity while encouraging creativity. Kids won't just color—they'll explore the people, places, and events that helped shape America.
---
---
---
Perfect for:* Home school families* Classroom enrichment* Summer learning* Family activity nights* Birthday and holiday gifts Instead of spending hours on a tablet, your child can spend hours creating colorful masterpieces while learning the incredible story of America.Give your child a fun way to celebrate America's 250th birthday—one page at a time!Order your copy of _Color Across America_ today and start your family's colorful journey through American history.Happy Coloring!Sincerely,Ingrid Centurion, LTC, USA (Ret.)Founder and President

name: Senator Katie Britt
subject: This Independence Day is unlike any other.
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Britt for Alabama, Inc
body:
250 years later, Freedom still endures

Peter,

This Independence Day is unlike any other.

As America celebrates the 250th anniversary of our nation's founding, we have
the opportunity to reflect on two and a half centuries of courage, sacrifice,
and the enduring promise of freedom.

On July 4, 1776, our Founding Fathers boldly declared that liberty was worth
fighting for. They affirmed that our rights come from God, not government, and
entrusted future generations with the responsibility of preserving a nation
built on faith, opportunity, and freedom.

Against incredible odds, they established a nation founded on liberty,
self-government, and the belief that freedom belongs to every American.

For 250 years, generations of Americans have carried that promise forward.
Through perseverance, innovation, faith, and an unwavering belief in freedom,
they have built stronger communities, expanded opportunity, and ensured that
the blessings of liberty would endure for future generations.

Today, we honor their service, celebrate the freedoms they secured, and
remember that America's story is still being written.

It is the honor of a lifetime to represent Alabama in the United States
Senate, and I remain committed to fighting for the principles that have made
our nation the greatest force for freedom and opportunity the world has ever
known.

As we celebrate America's 250th birthday, I hope you'll enjoy this special day
with your loved ones, reflect on the incredible blessings we share as
Americans, and look to the future with confidence. I truly believe our nation's
best days are still ahead of us.

From my family to yours, thank you for your continued support and for
everything you do to make America stronger each and every day.

May God bless you and your family, and may He continue to bless the United
States of America.

Happy Independence Day!

Sincerely,

Senator Katie Britt

| PPeter,

Happy Fourth of July!

Today, we celebrate the birth of our nation and the courage of those who fought to secure our independence nearly 250 years ago.

The freedoms we enjoy today did not come without tremendous sacrifice. Our freedom was hard-earned through tenacity, perseverance, and the belief that ordinary people could come together to build a better future.

As we gather with family and friends, let’s celebrate and remember that every generation has been called upon to defend and strengthen the promise of America.

Our founders fought for independence. Others fought to expand civil rights and secure voting rights. Along the way, every generation has been tested to defend our country.

**Now it's our turn.**

We cannot take our democracy, our freedoms, or our rights for granted. We must continue standing up for one another, strengthening our communities, and fighting for the values that make this country worth celebrating.

We know this work is not easy, and in countless ways it feels harder than ever to ensure America lives up to the promise of democracy. Thankfully, the resilience, persistence and bravery that made winning our independence possible is what it means to be American.

I hope you and your family have a safe and meaningful Fourth of July.

Happy Independence Day!

With gratitude,

Stefany

clean_body: | = | PPeter, Happy Fourth of July! Today, we celebrate the birth of our nation and the courage of those who fought to secure our independence nearly 250 years ago. The freedoms we enjoy today did not come without tremendous sacrifice. Our freedom was hard-earned through tenacity, perseverance, and the belief that ordinary people could come together to build a better future. As we gather with family and friends, let’s celebrate and remember that every generation has been called upon to defend and strengthen the promise of America. Our founders fought for independence. Others fought to expand civil rights and secure voting rights. Along the way, every generation has been tested to defend our country. Now it's our turn. We cannot take our democracy, our freedoms, or our rights for granted. We must continue standing up for one another, strengthening our communities, and fighting for the values that make this country worth celebrating. We know this work is not easy, and in countless ways it feels harder than ever to ensure America lives up to the promise of democracy. Thankfully, the resilience, persistence and bravery that made winning our independence possible is what it means to be American. I hope you and your family have a safe and meaningful Fourth of July. name: Abdul El-Sayed
subject: What do we want from the next 250?
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Abdul for U
body:
We have this opportunity in front of us, if we're willing to grasp it.
# [ ](https://act.abdulformichigan.com/go/1218?t=1&akid=2535%2E251025%2EjZIng0)
Peter, today marks America’s 250th anniversary.
I know the accident of history that allowed me to be born in this country. I know what my life would have been had I been born in the place where all of my cousins were born.
[](https://act.abdulformichigan.com/go/507?c0=em-ms-aes-20260704-1-ak.KRtIZA&amount=10&refcode=em20260704-2530&t=3&akid=2535%2E251025%2EjZIng0)
I know what America can do for somebody. I just know that too often, America does not do that for too many of her kids.
As many challenges and as many mistakes as our country has made, there is one thing that America does better than almost any other country: we have the capacity to correct.
Sometimes those corrections don't come fast enough. Sometimes they haven't come yet. **But the beautiful thing about America is that we have the capacity to fight for a better future.**
We cannot fix the history of the past 250 years, but I’ll be honest, the question for us is not about the past 250. **The question for us is what do we want from the next 250?**
This exercise in our democracy right now is about that future.
Are we willing to let them continue to rig a system so that the next 250 look like the past 250 — where the rich get what they want, and the rest do what they can?
Do we want an America where we make war simply because we can, even if we don't know how we're going to get out of it, and understand that it is deeply unjust to make war in the first place?
Do we want an America where people continue to have to fight against their employers who have all the power and all the benefits?
[](https://act.abdulformichigan.com/go/507?c0=em-ms-aes-20260704-1-ak.KRtIZA&amount=10&refcode=em20260704-2530&t=4&akid=2535%2E251025%2EjZIng0)
Or do we want an America where we are willing to come together beyond our differences, beyond our divides — reaching together across the divides they tell us we can't reach, a geography of race, of faith, of ethnicity, of sexual orientation?
We can have nice things. But we can't do it alone.
The lesson of the last 250 is this: **yes, America can correct — if we're willing to do the work of correcting her. That's what this campaign is about.**
[](https://act.abdulformichigan.com/go/507?c0=em-ms-aes-20260704-1-ak.KRtIZA&amount=10&refcode=em20260704-2530&t=5&akid=2535%2E251025%2EjZIng0)
That's what we're all here to do. Out of a belief in what we can yet be. A belief that a child growing up five minutes from here has no less right to a great education, an incredible future, and the healthcare they deserve than a child living twenty miles away.
A belief that we can be a force for good in the world if we're willing to hold ourselves accountable to the international law we helped to build in the first place.
**A belief that when our government works for us, we hold our economy accountable to creating opportunity for working people — not just for the folks who already have the money to buy off that government.**
We have this opportunity in front of us, if we're willing to grasp it.
Happy 4th of July, Peter. Thanks for sticking with us.
— Abdul
