name: Scott Wiener
subject: This Fourth of July, say no kings
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Scott WIENER FOR CONGRESS
body:
| | Peter, I shared the following thoughts exclusively with the San Francisco Examiner today in honor of the Fourth of July. I'd like to share them with you too. **This Fourth of July, say no kings**
By: Scott Wiener. | Special to the Examiner

It’s been 250 years since the Founding Fathers set out to build a new kind of country. Lately, it seems like it hasn’t been going that well.

The Declaration of Independence laid out a radical vision: a country ruled by human rights instead of divine right, a government whose power comes directly from the consent of the governed, and a guarantee that all people possess an innate right to “life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.”

In 2026, it often feels like that remarkable vision is slipping away. The president is openly seeking to consolidate unchecked power with help from Congress and the Supreme Court. A roving band of secret police is kidnapping and murdering civilians in broad daylight, spreading terror through our communities. The rights of women, LGBTQ people and immigrants are being severely curtailed.

The abuses the Founding Fathers fought against are rearing their ugly heads again today, and we need new tools to eradicate them. As we mark the 250th anniversary of our independence, I’m calling for the most American change possible: a check on government abuses of power called the No Kings Act — legislation I’m advancing this year to ensure accountability when federal officials violate your rights. You should be able to sue federal officials when they violate your rights.

As we mark the 250th anniversary of our independence, I’m calling for the most American change possible.

Though the Constitution guarantees a set of inalienable rights to all people on U.S. soil, it doesn’t say much about what you’re supposed to do when the federal government violates those rights.

For instance, there’s not much you can do if a federal officer yanks you from your car without a warrant, throws you to the ground, beats you and kidnaps you for several days so that you lose your job. That’s not a hypothetical — that happened to Marvin Godoy Calderon, a janitor with a valid U.S. work permit, in the Sunnyside district of San Francisco just weeks ago.

Or say you are a citizen and military veteran on your way to work, and you come across a group of law-enforcement officers conducting an immigration raid. Because you look Mexican, they tell you to pull over, smash your window, pepper-spray you, kneel on your neck, and kidnap you for 72 hours before releasing you with no apology. That happened to George Retes in Camarillo last summer.

Right now, there is no realistic path to get justice in either of those cases. You have a right to be protected from excessive force, wrongful arrest, or unreasonable search and seizure, and to have equal protection — but federal statute does not grant you the right to sue officers or their agencies when they violate those rights. You used to be able to file what’s called a Bivens lawsuit, but this right-wing Supreme Court gutted that ability a few years ago.

The Founding Fathers didn’t tolerate that kind of abusive, fascist behavior, and neither should we.

Next month, the California Legislature will take its final vote on my Senate Bill 747, the No Kings Act. It’s a first-of-its kind bill in the nation that establishes a cause of action in state law to file a lawsuit against any federal official who violates your constitutional rights.

For the first time, Californians will have the right to sue federal officials for a wide array of constitutional violations, whether it’s the Department of Justice targeting President Donald Trump’s political opponents, ICE illegally kidnapping and deporting people, or university grants that are terminated because of disfavored political views.

That accountability is incredibly powerful. It’s fundamental to a free society. Right now, many ICE agents don’t bother to show warrants for their arrests because there are no consequences if they don’t. If we want to end ICE’s terror campaign and this air of impunity — and the future of democracy depends on ending them — we must end the lack of accountability that drives such reckless, illegal behavior.

Some have argued that federal law prevents states like California from allowing people to sue the federal government. But there is a growing legal movement — one that includes several prominent Trump appointees in the federal courts — that believes states do have the power to allow these lawsuits.

Regardless of how the courts rule on my No Kings Act in California, we must pass a similar law at the national level to extend these protections to every state. I’m running for Congress in part to pass a federal No Kings Act and hold ICE and other Trump officials accountable for violating the Constitution.

The rights the Founding Fathers wrote about in the Declaration of Independence are more than a paper promise. To defend that founding rule-of-law vision today, we must ensure those rights have teeth.

**On this Fourth of July, as we celebrate 250 years of freedom from monarchy, we say again: no kings.** Have a happy and safe holiday -

clean_body: | | Peter, I shared the following thoughts exclusively with the San Francisco Examiner today in honor of the Fourth of July. I'd like to share them with you too. This Fourth of July, say no kings By: Scott Wiener. | Special to the Examiner It’s been 250 years since the Founding Fathers set out to build a new kind of country. Lately, it seems like it hasn’t been going that well. The Declaration of Independence laid out a radical vision: a country ruled by human rights instead of divine right, a government whose power comes directly from the consent of the governed, and a guarantee that all people possess an innate right to “life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.” In 2026, it often feels like that remarkable vision is slipping away. The president is openly seeking to consolidate unchecked power with help from Congress and the Supreme Court. A roving band of secret police is kidnapping and murdering civilians in broad daylight, spreading terror through our communities. The rights of women, LGBTQ people and immigrants are being severely curtailed. The abuses the Founding Fathers fought against are rearing their ugly heads again today, and we need new tools to eradicate them. As we mark the 250th anniversary of our independence, I’m calling for the most American change possible: a check on government abuses of power called the No Kings Act — legislation I’m advancing this year to ensure accountability when federal officials violate your rights. You should be able to sue federal officials when they violate your rights. As we mark the 250th anniversary of our independence, I’m calling for the most American change possible. Though the Constitution guarantees a set of inalienable rights to all people on U.S. soil, it doesn’t say much about what you’re supposed to do when the federal government violates those rights. For instance, there’s not much you can do if a federal officer yanks you from your car without a warrant, throws you to the ground, beats you and kidnaps you for several days so that you lose your job. That’s not a hypothetical — that happened to Marvin Godoy Calderon, a janitor with a valid U.S. work permit, in the Sunnyside district of San Francisco just weeks ago. Or say you are a citizen and military veteran on your way to work, and you come across a group of law-enforcement officers conducting an immigration raid. Because you look Mexican, they tell you to pull over, smash your window, pepper-spray you, kneel on your neck, and kidnap you for 72 hours before releasing you with no apology. That happened to George Retes in Camarillo last summer. Right now, there is no realistic path to get justice in either of those cases. You have a right to be protected from excessive force, wrongful arrest, or unreasonable search and seizure, and to have equal protection — but federal statute does not grant you the right to sue officers or their agencies when they violate those rights. You used to be able to file what’s called a Bivens lawsuit, but this right-wing Supreme Court gutted that ability a few years ago. The Founding Fathers didn’t tolerate that kind of abusive, fascist behavior, and neither should we. Next month, the California Legislature will take its final vote on my Senate Bill 747, the No Kings Act. It’s a first-of-its kind bill in the nation that establishes a cause of action in state law to file a lawsuit against any federal official who violates your constitutional rights. For the first time, Californians will have the right to sue federal officials for a wide array of constitutional violations, whether it’s the Department of Justice targeting President Donald Trump’s political opponents, ICE illegally kidnapping and deporting people, or university grants that are terminated because of disfavored political views. That accountability is incredibly powerful. It’s fundamental to a free society. Right now, many ICE agents don’t bother to show warrants for their arrests because there are no consequences if they don’t. If we want to end ICE’s terror campaign and this air of impunity — and the future of democracy depends on ending them — we must end the lack of accountability that drives such reckless, illegal behavior. Some have argued that federal law prevents states like California from allowing people to sue the federal government. But there is a growing legal movement — one that includes several prominent Trump appointees in the federal courts — that believes states do have the power to allow these lawsuits. Regardless of how the courts rule on my No Kings Act in California, we must pass a similar law at the national level to extend these protections to every state. I’m running for Congress in part to pass a federal No Kings Act and hold ICE and other Trump officials accountable for violating the Constitution. The rights the Founding Fathers wrote about in the Declaration of Independence are more than a paper promise. To defend that founding rule-of-law vision today, we must ensure those rights have teeth. On this Fourth of July, as we celebrate 250 years of freedom from monarchy, we say again: no kings. # CNN Legal Journalist Paula Reid Is Leaving for MS NOW — She Fears Paramount CEO Will Install Bari Weiss to Run CNN
---
CNN journalist Paula Reid is leaving the network for MS NOW out of concerns over Paramount Skydance's acquisition of the network, Fox News confirmed. "Reid turned down a chance to renew her current contract at CNN, according to two people familiar with the situation, in part because CNN's next era appears chaotic," Variety reported. Reid's decision allegedly came because of concerns over Paramount CEO David Ellison taking over the network and potentially installing CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss as head of CNN.
---
| | | | Key Takeaways ✓ CNN legal journalist Paula Reid is leaving for MS NOW, citing fears that Paramount CEO David Ellison will install CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss to run CNN after the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition closes.

✓ Reid's departure is among the most high-profile talent exits connected to CNN's pending merger — with Ellison's planned leadership reportedly creating the "chaotic" atmosphere that is driving multiple staff departures.

✓ The potential installation of Bari Weiss — a prominent journalist known for her criticism of mainstream media from a centrist-to-conservative perspective — as CNN's head would represent the most dramatic editorial direction change at a major US news network in years.
---
Ellison, who is set to run CNN once Paramount's purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery becomes official, has reportedly frightened many employees of the cable news network. Reid's departure is among the most high-profile in a wave of CNN talent exits connected to uncertainty over the network's post-merger direction.
---
